profile.summary: Software engineer with a background in numerical simulation of liquid-state chemical systems, with a focus on energy transfer applications. Experienced at designing and implementing novel algorithms to improve the accuracy of both quantum and classical simulations in an efficient manner on modern high performance computing platforms. Skilled at analyzing complex problems, identifying and implementing effective solutions.

positions.description: Leading the creation, implementation, and optimization of software tools and algorithms in support of multiple domains, including semiconductor design, manufacturing, and validation, and enabling our engineering partners to produce critical silicon devices and integrated products.

positions.title: Postdoctoral Researcher
positions.description:
Performed numerical simulations and detailed analysis of the structure and electronic properties of organic polymers with applications to photovoltaic technologies, ultimately identifying liquid interfaces as a major driver of chain conformations and excitation spectra.

In particular, I studied the effects of bulk aggregation and polymer chain conformations on the excitonic behavior of poly-3-hexylthiophene (P3HT), using multiple techniques, including numerical simulations of both atomistic and coarse-grained models of large polymer aggregates within GROMACS. Correlations between polymer backbone configurations and electronic structure were elucidated using semi-empirical PPP Hamiltonians for efficient electronic structure analysis, and I developed an extensive library of aggregated chain structures to use in training LSTM models to allow prediction of excitonic spectra directly from the output of coarse-grained simulations. Once we identified the inter-monomer dihedral angle as a key parameter governing electronic structure (owing to its effect on chain conjugation), the model was able to predict these exciation energies with > 90% accuracy.

Using a variety of simulation and analysis techniques, including free energy methods and structural order parameters, I was able to examine the aggregation behavior of several competing polymer models and identify their strengths and weaknesses, enabling us to refine our own coarse-grained model to obtain high fidelity in reproducing the critical dihedral angles measured in experiments while retaining the improved simulation efficiency stemming from reduced structural complexity. In turn, this motivated a closer look at aggregation results from the literature, leading to the discovery of the significant forcing effects of liquid-vapor interfaces on chain conformation and providing insight into a possible source of nucleation sites for the crystalline domains suspected to be critical for efficient solar energy conversion.

positions.title: Research Assistant
positions.description:
Designed and developed highly-scalable C++/MPI code to perform some of the first truly rigorous and accurate quantum-classical simulations of proton transfer reactions in atomistically detailed liquid environments.

The code developed for this project included both a core I developed to implement our new approach to quantum simulations along with a plug-in module to enable connectivity with the LAMMPS molecular dynamics engine, a large, extensible open-source simulation tool written in C/C++, frequently used in the chemistry and materials science research communities. Using a hierarchical MPI+MPI communication algorithm, it was possible to scale the combined application to thousands of HPC cores, enabling rigorous quantum simulations of unprecedented size. The performance of the system was further improved by implementing a variety of methods developed in our group over the course of the research, leveraging maximally compact basis sets, tensor propagator techniques, quasi-adiabatic references with ensemble averaging, reference hopping, and path filtering, allowing for hundreds of picoseconds of simulation across hundreds of atoms.

During this time, I also developed a novel, noise-insensitive numerical method for extracting simple harmonic bath parameters from short classical simulations, allowing even larger systems (such as full photosynthetic protein units) to be characterized using state of the art influence functional tensor methods, enabling a deeper understanding of the effects of protein structure and solvent environment on quantum transport of energetic excitations, e.g. in photosynthesis.

To further these lines of research, I received a Blue Waters Graduate Fellowship, provided jointly by the NSF and NCSA and offering both a stipend and time grants on the flagship NCSA Blue Waters supercomputer and enabling our lab to fully leverage advanced computing resources to address these cutting-edge problems.
